gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the EG4 6000XP's 6,000 W is split into two 120 V legs of 3,000 W each, with no balancing between them. One 120 V leg overloads at just over 3,000 W even when the total load is well under 6,000 W. ChatGPT's $750 Growatt SPF 5000US card is a 240 V-only unit that needs a separate transformer before it can feed ordinary 120 V outlets.
standout_why: I opened five pages. The cited EG4 6000XP product page says only 'Don't compromise on surge capacity and line imbalance capability', with no number. liveoffthegrid.com/specs, solarspecdb.com and signaturesolarsolutions.com list only '6,000 W continuous, 120/240 V split phase'. wildjoule.com/best-off-grid-inverter covers surge, idle draw and LF vs HF but gives only total split-phase ratings and never mentions per-leg limits or neutral-ground bonding. None of these says the Growatt card is 240 V-only. I did not open storyofsolar.com, the off-the-grid-solar.com collection or device.report (403).
decides: A typical US off-grid home runs mostly 120 V loads: fridge, microwave, space heater, 120 V well pump. On the 6000XP these must be split across L1 and L2 so neither leg goes over 3,000 W. For example, an 1,800 W microwave plus a 1,500 W heater on the same leg is 3,300 W. That overloads the leg even though it is only 55% of the 6,000 W rating. A buyer with heavy 120 V loads should balance the circuits, add a second unit, or pick a unit that can carry more on one leg. ChatGPT's Growatt SPF 5000US card ($750) puts out 230/240 V only, so one unit cannot power a US 120 V panel without the Growatt ATS 5000T-ES transformer. That rules it out as a drop-in answer for a US cabin or home. The 6000XP stays the simplest single-box split-phase pick, but only when it is sized by leg, not by total watts.

findings.label: Max continuous line (per-leg) wattage
findings.value: 3,000 W per 120 V line (6,000 W nominal total)
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP User Manual, page 5 (Technical Specifications), ManualsLib
findings.note: The page's text extraction separates labels from values. The label order is 'OUTPUT VOLTAGE, OUTPUT FREQUENCY, MAX. CONTINUOUS OUTPUT CURRENT @ 240V, MAX CONT. LINE WATTAGE, NOMINAL POWER OUTPUT'. The output values follow in matching order: '120/240VAC 50/60Hz ... 3000W 6000W'. So 3000W maps to MAX CONT. LINE WATTAGE and 6000W to NOMINAL POWER OUTPUT. The EG4 spec-sheet PDF would not parse to text, so I used the manual.

findings.label: Inverter topology
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP All-In-One Off-Grid Inverter - EG4 Electronics
findings.note: Maker's wording: 'This transformerless, high-frequency inverter'. Without an output transformer there is nothing to shift power between legs, which is consistent with the fixed 3,000 W per-line rating. The page names 'line imbalance capability' but gives no number.

findings.label: Neutral-ground bond
findings.value: Internal bond is off by default and can be switched on with setting 26 when there is no bond elsewhere in the system
findings.note: Manual wording: 'the 6000XP can be configured to create the bond internally (see setting 26).' An off-grid system with no utility service has no other bond, so the installer must either turn on setting 26 or bond at the panel. Doing both creates a second bond.

findings.label: PV input voltage
findings.value: 100–480 V DC input range; 120–385 V MPP operating range; 8,000 W usable (4,000 W per MPPT)
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP User Manual, page 5 (Technical Specifications), ManualsLib
findings.note: Cold-weather Voc must stay under 480 V (manual page 16: 'does not exceed the inverter's maximum input voltage of 480VDC').

findings.label: Idle consumption
findings.value: <30 W with PV; ≈50 W on battery; <50 W with AC
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP User Manual, page 5 (Technical Specifications), ManualsLib
findings.note: Footnote on page 6: '*Idle consumption value tested with constant 300VDC PV source'. 50 W × 24 h = 1.2 kWh/day on battery.
